notes.meaning: As the church in Jerusalem grew rapidly, tension arose between two groups of Jewish believers. The Greek-speaking Jews complained that their widows were being overlooked in the daily food distribution. The apostles recognized this as a serious matter that needed a fair and orderly solution.

The twelve apostles called the whole congregation together to address the problem. They explained that their primary calling was to preach God's message, not to manage money or food distribution. Stepping away from preaching the word would hurt the main mission Christ gave them.

The apostles told the believers to choose seven trusted men from among themselves. These men needed to have good reputations and be full of the Holy Spirit and practical wisdom. The congregation would select them, and the apostles would officially place them in charge of this work.

By handing over the daily charity work, the apostles could focus entirely on their main duties. They planned to give their full time and energy to prayer and to preaching God's word. Preaching needed to be supported by constant prayer if it was going to touch and change people's hearts.

The whole congregation liked the plan and selected seven men, beginning with Stephen, who was known for deep faith and the Spirit's power. All seven had Greek names, showing great care for the Greek-speaking group that had felt overlooked. One of them, Nicolas, was a convert from Antioch who had previously joined the Jewish faith.

differ.view: These seven men were the first deacons, establishing the official church office dedicated to caring for the poor.
These men were not formal deacons, but temporary problem-solvers or leaders closer to elders, since Stephen and Philip were public preachers and the text does not give them an official title.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Church tradition holds that this was the ordination of the first deacons, an order of clergy that serves the church.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Stephen is honored as the Archdeacon because he was the chief of the original seven deacons appointed here.

notes.meaning: The chosen men were brought before the apostles, who prayed for them and placed their hands on them. This laying on of hands was a public sign setting them apart for their special task and asking God to bless their service. It gave them clear authority from the apostles to handle the church's daily care.

differ.view: The apostles' laying on of hands actually passed on miraculous spiritual gifts to these men, enabling them to do signs and wonders.

notes.meaning: With the internal dispute peacefully resolved, God's message continued to spread with great power. Many more people in Jerusalem became followers of Jesus, and even a large company of Jewish priests believed. Their faith showed that God was reaching those who had once resisted the Christian message.

Stephen did not limit his service to handing out food, because God gave him great grace and spiritual power. He began performing amazing signs and miracles openly among the people. These wonders confirmed that the message he shared about Jesus was truly from God.

Opposition soon arose from foreign Jews worshiping at a synagogue made up of freed slaves and men from North Africa and Asia Minor. Saul of Tarsus may well have attended, since his home region of Cilicia is named. These men began debating Stephen, trying to disprove his message about Jesus.

Stephen's opponents were completely unable to win the argument against him. The Holy Spirit gave him deep wisdom and knowledge of Scripture that they could not match or answer. Jesus was keeping His promise to give His followers words that enemies could not resist.

Having lost the debate, Stephen's enemies secretly persuaded men to tell lies about him. They accused him of speaking blasphemy—words that insult or dishonor God and Moses. Under Jewish law, a charge of blasphemy was a terrible crime punishable by death.

The accusers stirred up the general public along with the local Jewish elders and religious teachers. They rushed at Stephen, grabbed him violently, and dragged him before the Sanhedrin, the Jewish high court. This was the first time that the Jerusalem crowds joined the leaders against the disciples.

The accusers brought forward dishonest witnesses to claim that Stephen continually attacked the temple and the law of Moses. They twisted what he actually said, making it sound as if Jesus planned to ruin the holy place and wipe out their sacred customs. Stephen had simply taught that Jesus fulfilled the true meaning of the temple and the law.

Everyone in the council stared at Stephen and saw that his face looked like the face of an angel. God gave him a calm, fearless peace and a heavenly glow, showing that he was pure and innocent. This quiet brightness was a sign that God stood with him, just as He had once made the face of Moses shine.
